title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models
abstract: What if language models could think AND act? ReAct combines two previously separate capabilities—reasoning traces (like chain-of-thought) and task-specific actions (like API calls)—into an interleaved dance. The result: models that can plan, gather information from the real world, update their plans, and solve complex tasks with human-like interpretability. On benchmarks from question-answering to web shopping, ReAct achieves state-of-the-art performance while producing trajectories humans can actually understand and trust.

sections.title: The Core Insight
sections.content:
Imagine you're researching a complex question. You don't just think silently in your head—you Google things, read articles, and update your understanding. You don't just click around blindly either—you reason about what to search for next.

Language models have been doing these separately. Chain-of-thought prompting helps them reason step-by-step, but they can hallucinate facts they don't actually know. Action-based agents can use tools and APIs, but without reasoning, they stumble through tasks without a plan.

ReAct's key insight: interleave thinking and doing. Generate a thought, take an action, observe the result, think again. This creates a feedback loop where reasoning guides actions, and actions ground reasoning in reality.

visualization.description: The ReAct loop: Think → Act → Observe → Think again

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content:
A ReAct prompt teaches the model by example. You show it a few solved problems where a human wrote out their thoughts (what am I trying to figure out?), actions (let me search for X), and observations (the search returned Y).

For question answering, actions might be: Search[entity] to look something up, or Lookup[keyword] to find specific info in the current page. The model learns to use these tools strategically.

Here's the magic: with just 1-2 examples, the model generalizes to new problems. It learns the pattern of interleaved reasoning and acting, not just the specific content.

visualization.description: ReAct architecture: Language model with reasoning and action heads

sections.title: Benchmark Results
sections.content:
ReAct was tested on four diverse benchmarks spanning knowledge tasks and decision making:

HotpotQA (multi-hop QA): ReAct achieved 27% exact match vs 25% for Chain-of-Thought, while producing fewer hallucinated facts.

Fever (fact verification): Similar improvements with better calibration—when ReAct is wrong, it's often because the retrieved evidence was insufficient, not because of hallucination.

ALFWorld (text game): 71% success rate, a massive 34% absolute improvement over imitation learning baselines.

WebShop (web shopping): 40% success rate, 10% better than baselines, approaching human performance of 59%.

sections.title: Why Reasoning + Acting Synergize
sections.content:
The combination is more powerful than either alone. Consider what goes wrong with each approach in isolation:

Reasoning-only (Chain-of-Thought) can generate plausible-sounding but factually incorrect reasoning. The model confidently states things it doesn't actually know, with no way to verify against reality.

Acting-only gathers real information but can't synthesize it. The model might retrieve all the right facts but fail to combine them into an answer.

ReAct gets the best of both: actions ground the reasoning in real retrieved facts, while reasoning helps the model decide what to retrieve next and synthesize the results.

sections.title: Human Interpretability
sections.content:
Perhaps the most underrated benefit of ReAct: you can actually read what the model is thinking.

Each trajectory shows the model's reasoning in natural language. When it makes a mistake, you can pinpoint exactly where things went wrong. Was it a bad search query? Misinterpretation of results? Flawed reasoning?

This opens the door to a new form of human-AI collaboration. In the paper's experiments, when ReAct failed on ALFWorld tasks, humans could fix the behavior by editing just 1-2 thoughts. The reasoning traces become an interface for steering the model.

This interpretability isn't just nice to have—it's essential for building AI systems we can trust and debug in production.

sections.title: Impact and What Came Next
sections.content:
ReAct became a foundational pattern for LLM agents. Its influence spans:

LangChain and agent frameworks: The ReAct pattern is now a standard agent type, used by thousands of developers.

Tool-using LLMs: GPT-4, Claude, and other models now routinely combine reasoning with tool use, following ReAct's blueprint.

Research directions: Papers like Reflexion, AutoGPT, and HuggingGPT build on ReAct's core insight of interleaved thinking and acting.

The paper's lasting contribution isn't just a technique—it's a mental model for how language models should interact with the world: think, act, observe, repeat.
